records.english:
On the author's words “Similarly, with respect to its matter, it is divided into the five arts”: the logician must investigate the matter of syllogism just as he investigates its form. Logic provides protection against error in both respects. Through logic we learn, for example, that the matter of a definition is its genus and differentia and that its form requires the former to precede the latter; and that the matter of a demonstration consists of certain premises, while its form is one of the four syllogistic figures.

The possibility of acquiring theoretical knowledge from immediate or necessary cognitions is self-evident. But theoretical questions are exceedingly numerous, and one cannot acquire any desired theorem from just any self-evident proposition. The investigator must obtain, for each kind of theoretical question, initial cognitions possessing a particular suitability to that question. Genus and differentia suit the disclosure of a species' quiddity; certain premises containing the requisite terms suit a demonstrative conclusion; generally accepted premises suit dialectic; and probable premises suit rhetorical reasoning. Even when the appropriate cognitions have been obtained, the investigator cannot derive the desired result by arranging them in whatever fashion he pleases. He must follow a determinate procedure with its particular conditions and order: for forming a conception, the defining expression must be coextensive with what it defines and prior to it in knowledge; for assent by the first figure, the minor premise must be affirmative and the major universal.

Those prior cognitions which have a special suitability to the proposed conclusion, rather than to just any conclusion, are its *matter*. The required method of ordering and combining them is its *form*. Neither the correct choice of matter nor the correct choice of form is altogether self-evident. Were it so, eminent scholars would not fall into error or quarrel as they do: philosophers dispute questions of metaphysics and natural philosophy, while Muslim scholars differ over the principles of jurisprudence and particular legal rulings. Indeed, scholars accuse one another of error sometimes in the material premises and sometimes in the form of inference. Each therefore needs general rules by which it may be properly secured.

The opening of this gloss already explained that thought has two movements. The first seeks and obtains the material of an inference; the second arranges that material in the required form. The second movement plainly needs rules by which an appropriate figure can be constructed for each desired conclusion, and the first needs rules no less. Consequently the discussions of the five arts—how the principles of demonstration, dialectic and the other arts are obtained and distinguished—form part of logic. Without these discussions another science would be needed to guard thinking against material error. To claim that the suitability of every principle to every inquiry is self-evident is almost as hopeless as stripping the thorns from a thornbush. Logic therefore undertakes protection against errors both of matter and of form.

It is a serious mistake to say that logic guards only the form, whereas the matter of each proposition can be known solely through the special science concerned with it. Nor does one prove this by pointing to disagreements among scholars familiar with logic. For instance, scholars have differed over whether pouring the water of one vessel into two vessels annihilates the one individual portion and produces two new individuals, or whether the former individual survives and only its quality of connectedness disappears. Each party has claimed its own view to be immediately evident. But the safeguard against error is not the mere possession of logic: it is *observing its rules*. When learned investigators disagree, one or both parties may have failed to observe those rules adequately.

An example will make this clear. Rational investigators disagree about whether the world is eternal. One argument for eternity runs: “The world is an effect of the Necessary Existent; every effect of the Necessary Existent is eternal; therefore the world is eternal.” Its major premise, however, is open to denial. What is genuinely self-evident does not admit such a challenge. The error is to treat a premise that is merely probable as if it supplied demonstration, overlooking logic's requirement that a demonstration be built from necessary and certain premises.

The discussion must nevertheless distinguish the *general criteria supplied by logic* from the ascertainment of particular premises. The gloss mentions “animal” as a genus of human beings and “rational” as a differentia, and the familiar material for arguing that the world is originated: “The world changes; every changing thing is originated; therefore the world is originated.” Logic supplies the general rule that a genus is a shared essential attribute and a differentia a distinguishing essential attribute. To apply the rule, we still have to investigate the essential and accidental features of human beings and establish, as a minor premise, that animality is an essential attribute shared with other species. Coupled with “every such shared essential is a genus,” this yields “animal is a genus.” The same procedure applies to “rational” as differentia.

Likewise logic teaches, as a general rule, that demonstrative premises must be self-evident or certain. When we investigate the premises proposed for the world's origination, we must ascertain whether they really possess that certainty. If two premises do, we may argue: “These two premises are certain; every pair of premises of that kind supplies demonstration; therefore these two premises supply demonstration.” We have dwelt at length on this question because it is a place where one's footing easily slips. From God alone come success and protection.

There is an evident difficulty in the preceding classification. It appears to imply that fallacious reasoning also consists of firm but non-certain assent, except that, unlike dialectic, it requires neither public acceptance of the premises nor concession by the opponent. On its face this is false. A sophistical argument is composed either of estimative premises (*wahmiyyāt*) or of premises deceptively resembling sound ones (*mushabbahāt*); neither type, as such, supplies genuine firm assent. One might reply that such premises are *presented in the manner of decisive assertions*, even though they do not correspond to reality.

However that may be, a clearer ordering of the five arts would proceed as follows. First ask whether the arranged premises involve judgment and assent. If they do not, their arrangement belongs to *poetic reasoning*. If they do, ask whether the inquiry is conducted with the aim of avoiding or exposing such premises: where that is the object, we have *fallacy or sophistry*. Otherwise ask whether the assent is decisive or only probable. If it is probable, the reasoning is *rhetorical*. If it is decisive, ask whether it is accompanied by certainty: with certainty it is *demonstrative*; without certainty it is *dialectical*.

This division, moreover, is not a strictly rationally exhaustive division but an *inductive* enumeration. Premises which lack judgment and assent include more than imaginative premises alone: they could belong to some other class as well. A purportedly exhaustive logical dichotomy has therefore not been established.

The name refers to a demonstration of *that something is the case* (*burhān innī*): it establishes the existence or actuality of the judgment in the world, without disclosing the cause that makes it so. In this kind of inference one proceeds from an effect toward its cause. Its name may be derived from the particle *inna*, one of the particles resembling verbs, because *inna* conveys affirmation and establishment. Alternatively it may be derived from *anā*, “I,” because that pronoun signifies an individuated and determinate subject; on the latter explanation the doubling of the nūn is accounted for as in the earlier discussion of the corresponding *limmī* demonstration. These are the glossator's reported explanations of the technical name, not a separate proof of the causal inference.

Jurists, for example, may establish a ruling by a report transmitted through a single narrator, once the permissibility of acting upon such a report has already been established in the science of legal theory (*uṣūl al-fiqh*). Within a dialectical argument constructed on that concession, an opponent may not simply answer that acting on a single-narrator report is inadmissible: its admissibility is among the premises temporarily granted for the argument.

Similarly, students of literary expression may reject the coordination in a line attributed to Abū Tammām: “No, by Him who knows that the *nadā* is bitter aloe and that Abū al-Ḥusayn is generous.” Their objection is that the two coordinated statements lack an appropriate unifying relation (*jiha jāmiʿa*). This argument presupposes the rule already accepted in the science of meanings (*ʿilm al-maʿānī*): coordination by *wāw* is acceptable only when there is such a connection between the coordinated elements. If that rule has been conceded, the argument proceeds by applying it to the verse. The ambiguous poetic nouns are retained here as features of the cited wording, not independently adjudicated lexical readings.

The explanation is that probable propositions (*maẓnūnāt*) form a wider class than accepted propositions (*maqbūlāt*), as was mentioned earlier. When the former are coordinated with the latter, the intended meaning is the remainder of the wider class after its narrower kind has been set aside: probable propositions *other than* the accepted ones. The same explanation applies whenever a more general term is joined in speech to one of its species.

The purpose of rhetorical reasoning is to encourage people toward things beneficial to them in this life and in the life to come, as preachers and exhorters do. It seeks persuasion and motivation, rather than the specifically demonstrative certainty associated with *burhān*.

A fallacy may arise either from the *form* of the argument or from its *matter*.

A formal fallacy occurs when the argument lacks a productive figure, either because the middle term is not genuinely repeated or because one of the required conditions concerning quantity, affirmative or negative quality, or modality is not observed. The first defect appears in an argument such as: “Every human has hair; every hair grows from a place; therefore every human grows from a place.” The middle expression has not been used in the same predicative relation. Similarly: “The knife is in the melon; the melon grows in the garden; therefore the knife grows in the garden.” The relation expressed in one premise is not the relation needed in the next.

Defects in the conditions of the figure include the following. “Every human is an animal; some animals are horses; therefore some humans are horses” fails because the major premise is not universal. “No human is a horse; every horse is an animal; therefore no human is an animal” fails because the minor premise is negative, whereas the relevant first-figure inference requires an affirmative minor. In the modal example already considered, “Every donkey that actually exists is a possible mount of Zayd; everything Zayd actually rides is necessarily a horse; therefore every donkey is necessarily a horse,” the claimed conclusion fails because the minor does not establish the needed *actual* predication: mere possibility of being ridden by Zayd cannot function as an actual bridge to the second premise. These examples concern the first figure; corresponding restrictions apply to the other figures as well.

A defect of *matter*, according to the customary classification being reported, can arise from wording or from meaning. Under verbal defects one may include *begging the question* (*muṣādara ʿalā al-maṭlūb*), where the desired conclusion and some premise amount to one and the same thing. The gloss offers: “Every human is a person; every person laughs; therefore every human laughs.” It also gives equivocation in the middle term: “This is an *ʿayn*,” pointing to gold; “Every *ʿayn* weeps,” referring instead to an eye; “therefore this weeps.” The middle expression *ʿayn* has changed meaning from gold to the organ of sight.

An alleged defect of meaning is exemplified by a horse depicted on a wall: “This is a horse; every horse neighs; therefore this [image] neighs.” The predication is shifted from the pictured likeness to a living animal. Other scholars count as material mistakes the transfer of a judgment from a species to its genus: “This is a colour; colour is black; therefore this is black.” They also count transferring a judgment made under a qualification to something unqualified: “This is a slave; the slave is a believer; therefore this one is a believer”; or treating a man with impaired night vision as if the unqualified predicate “sees” implied “sees at night.” Likewise they warn against replacing a *natural proposition* about a nature itself with a *universal* proposition about its bearers: “Human is animal; animal is a genus; therefore human is a genus.”

The glossator's own judgment, however, is that these latter examples are fundamentally defective in *form and arrangement*: in every case the alleged major lacks the universality required for the conclusion. He finds it surprising that some investigators themselves acknowledge this defect yet still place the examples in the chapter on material fallacies. The rival classifications should be kept distinct rather than silently assimilated.

For a verbal fallacy, the glossator gives the painted-horse example: one calls the image of a horse on a wall “a horse,” then combines that description with “every horse neighs” and infers that the image itself neighs.

For a fallacy of meaning, he gives an example in which the existential requirement on an affirmative proposition is neglected: “Everything that is both a human and a horse is human; everything that is both a human and a horse is a horse; therefore some human is a horse.” The inference fails because there is no existent bearer of the common subject “human-and-horse.” Nothing actually satisfies both titles, and the affirmative premises cannot supply the required existential witness.

Know that, among the five logical arts, the principal and most reliable one is *demonstration* (*burhān*). By it true convictions are attained and false convictions dispelled. One may also employ rhetoric or dialectic, but only demonstration, in this classification, yields certainty. Some interpreters have understood the Qurʾānic command, “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good exhortation, and dispute with them in the best manner” (Q 16:125), to allude to these arts: wisdom to demonstration, exhortation to rhetoric, and disputation to dialectic. The glossator reports this as an interpretation, not as a proof that the Qurʾānic terms are identical with the later technical classes.
